title: Rome's living judge — Pope or Council — is not even certain inside Rome
source_text: XL. Sed regerunt adversarii, si haeremus, num aliquid traditio sit Apostolica, & propter dissentientes veterum sententias res incerta videtur, in Ecclesia est certa authoritas quae dubium tollere possit, & cujus judicio verae traditiones a falsis discernantur, & fidelibus innotescant certo & infallibiliter. Si autem rogamus quis sit tanta authoritate praeditus, quum nulli amplius sint in Ecclesia viri a Deo inspirati, ut Prophetae & Apostoli, non omnes Adversarii eodem modo respondent. Nam eorum plerique dicunt authoritatem illam in Pontifice Romano residere, quem, scilicet, volunt judicem infallibilem esse in rebus fidei a Christo constitutum. Verum haec authoritas in ipsa Ecclesia Romana certa non est. Nec enim illi ipsi qui Pontifici Romano maxime adulantur, audent asserere hoc esse dogma de fide compertum atque manifestum. Siquidem non pauci sunt quos Ecclesia Romana pro Catholicis habet, & qui in ejus communione manent, qui in Papa non agnoscunt ejusmodi authoritatem. Alii vero contendunt praerogativam istam infallibilitatis in judicando de rebus fidei reperiri in Concilio, id est, in coetu generali praepositorum Ecclesiae. Sed rursus apud Ecclesiam Romanam istud adhuc minus certum est. Nam Pontificii plurimi reclamant, praecipue vero ipsi Romani Pontifices. Nec qui hoc negat ab ullo habetur in Ecclesia Romana haereticus. At, inquies, saltem omnes Pontificii consentiunt Concilia generalia quae Papa probavit atque confirmavit in fide errare non posse, & tuto eis posse credi. Verum, si Concilia quantumvis generalia non sint extra omne erroris periculum ante Papae confirmationem, & Papa ipse non sit infallibilis, quomodo infallibiliter judicabit an propositum Concilium erraverit, vel non?
pass_a_gloss: But the adversaries retort: if we hesitate whether any tradition is Apostolic, and because of the dissenting opinions of the ancients the matter seems uncertain, there is in the Church a certain authority that can remove the doubt, and by whose judgment true traditions are discerned from false, and made known to the faithful certainly and infallibly. But if we ask who is endowed with such great authority, since there are no longer in the Church men inspired by God as the Prophets and Apostles were, not all the Adversaries answer in the same way. For most of them say that authority resides in the Roman Pontiff, whom they will to be an infallible judge in matters of faith constituted by Christ. But this authority is not certain even in the Roman Church itself. For not even those who most flatter the Roman Pontiff dare assert that this is a dogma of the faith ascertained and manifest. Since indeed there are not a few whom the Roman Church holds as Catholics, and who remain in her communion, who do not acknowledge such authority in the Pope. Others contend that that prerogative of infallibility in judging matters of faith is found in a Council, that is, in a general assembly of the Church's overseers. But again among the Roman Church that is still less certain. For many Pontiffs protest, and especially the Roman Pontiffs themselves. Nor is anyone who denies this held a heretic in the Roman Church by anyone. But, you will say, at least all the Pontiffs agree that general Councils which the Pope has approved and confirmed cannot err in the faith, and can safely be believed. But if Councils, however general, are not beyond all danger of error before the Pope's confirmation, and the Pope himself is not infallible, how will he judge infallibly whether a proposed Council has erred or not?
pass_b_english: Rome replies: when ancients disagree and apostolic tradition looks uncertain, the Church has a living authority that can settle true vs false traditions for the faithful, certainly and infallibly.
Ask who holds that authority now that prophets and apostles are gone, and Rome splits.
Most say the Roman Pontiff is Christ's infallible faith-judge — yet even inside Rome that claim is not a settled de fide dogma; many Catholics in communion deny it.
Others put infallibility in a general Council of overseers — still less settled; many Roman doctors, and the popes themselves, fight it, and denying it is not treated as heresy.

The fallback — Councils safe once the Pope confirms them — collapses into a circle: if Councils can err before confirmation and the Pope is not infallible, how can he infallibly judge whether the Council erred?
